title: Data from Removable Media
summary: Data from removable media describes collecting information from storage that is attached to or inserted in a compromised computer, such as optical discs, memory cards, and Universal Serial Bus drives. The intruder needs no malware for this: ordinary shell commands list drives, enumerate files, and copy interesting items to a staging location before exfiltration. Because the media is local, the collection can avoid network-based monitoring entirely, and the strongest evidence therefore sits at the endpoint. File access records on the external volume, device insertion and removal events, and process lineage showing a scripting or file-copy utility touching a removable drive are the usual clues. The behaviour is hard to separate from legitimate backup or file transfer work, so volume identifiers, the account involved, and the volume of files read matter more than the action alone.

beginner.definition: Removable media is any storage you can plug in or take out. Examples are a USB stick, a memory card, or a CD. This technique means an attacker looks through those devices for useful files. They copy what they find so they can steal it later.
beginner.whyItMatters: A USB stick can hold a lot of private data and leaves the building in a pocket. The files never travel over the network, so network tools may see nothing. Attackers often gather files first and send them out later in one go. If you ignore local drives, a quiet copy of your most sensitive files can happen.
howItWorks: The attacker checks which drives are connected, including memory cards and optical discs.
They list folders and search for names that look valuable, such as finance or passwords.
They copy the chosen files to a folder on the same computer or the removable drive.
If many files are involved, an automated collection tool may do the copying.
The data is often packed into an archive so it can leave in one piece later.
Because the copy stays local, network monitoring may never see the files move.
beginner.example: Picture a post office worker who empties a sorting room. Boxes arrive from everywhere and wait to be sent on. A thief with a staff badge does not take boxes out of the front door. They fill a rucksack from the shelves and walk out at lunchtime. The cameras see only a normal employee leaving.
takeaways: Removable media collection happens on the endpoint, so network logs may show nothing.
Watch for file reads and copies on external volumes by unusual accounts or programs.
Device insertion records plus file access records together tell a clearer story.

objectives: Explain what removable media is and why attackers search it for data.
Describe the common steps of collecting files from a local drive or USB device.
Identify endpoint artefacts that show files were read from removable media.
Explain why network monitoring alone may not reveal this activity.
Describe how to tell routine file transfers from suspicious bulk collection.
